claim: The ANCH sequence is retained during reverse transcription of HIV-1.
source: Thus, the ANCH sequence is retained during reverse transcription, and this approach can be used to detect HIV-1 cDNA during the early replication phase.
evidence: The manuscript describes experiments showing eGFP.OR3 punctae in cells transduced with ANCH-containing vectors, demonstrating retention of the sequence.

claim: Integrated HIV-1 DNA can be detected using the ANCHOR system.
source: Of note, the eGFP.OR3 signal was stable for more than 4 weeks (when unintegrated viral cDNA species are expected to be degraded) suggesting that integrated viral DNA can be detected.
evidence: The stability of eGFP.OR3 signal over 4 weeks, when unintegrated DNA would be degraded, supports detection of integrated DNA.

claim: Nuclear eGFP.OR3 punctae were clearly detected in the nuclei of TZM-bl cells infected with HIV ANCH.
source: Distinct infection-induced eGFP punctae were clearly detected in the nuclei of these cells, but were not observed in the cytoplasm where eGFP.OR3 was diffusely distributed (Figure 1b).
evidence: Figure 1b shows nuclear eGFP.OR3 punctae in infected cells.

claim: Integrated proviral DNA was readily detected in HIV ANCH infected SupT1 cells.
source: Integrated proviral DNA was readily detected in HIV ANCH infected SupT1 cells, but was not observed when infection was performed in the presence of an RT- or IN-inhibitor (Figure 1c).
evidence: Alu-PCR data showing integrated DNA in infected cells but not in inhibitor-treated cells.

claim: Total HIV-1 cDNA levels became saturated at 10 hr post infection.
source: Total cDNA levels became saturated at 10 hr post infection (h p.i.) and 2-LTR circles peaked at 24 h p.i.; both species strongly declined over the following 5 days (Figure 1e).
evidence: ddPCR quantification data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: 2-LTR circles peaked at 24 h post infection.
source: Total cDNA levels became saturated at 10 hr post infection (h p.i.) and 2-LTR circles peaked at 24 h p.i.; both species strongly declined over the following 5 days (Figure 1e).
evidence: ddPCR quantification data shown in Figure 1e.

claim: eGFP.OR3 punctae increased over the first 72 hr and remained stable over the following 3 days despite the loss of HIV-1 cDNA species.
source: eGFP punctae, on the other hand, increased over the first 72 hr, but then remained stable over the following 3 days despite the observed loss of HIV-1 cDNA species (Figure 1d).
evidence: Quantification of eGFP.OR3 punctae over time shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Integrated HIV-1 DNA can be detected using the ANCHOR system.
source: Taken together, these results clearly indicated that integrated HIV-1 DNA can be detected using the ANCHOR system.
evidence: Stability of eGFP.OR3 punctae over time when unintegrated DNA declines supports detection of integrated DNA.

claim: Unintegrated HIV-1 cDNA is detected by the ANCHOR system.
source: TZM-bl eGFP.OR3 cells infected with VSV-G pseudotyped NNHIV ANCH also showed nuclear eGFP.OR3 punctae (Figure 1f–h) indicating that unintegrated HIV-1 cDNA is detected by the ANCHOR system as well.
evidence: NNHIV ANCH is integration-deficient, so eGFP.OR3 punctae in these infections represent unintegrated DNA.

claim: eGFP.OR3 punctae were not detected when cells were treated with NNHIV ANCH lacking VSV-G.
source: eGFP.OR3 punctae were not detected when cells were treated with NNHIV ANCH lacking VSV-G and were absent or strongly reduced in the presence of the RT inhibitors efavirenz (EFV) or azidothymidine (AZT) (Figure 1f and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Experimental data showing dependence on fusion and reverse transcription.

claim: eGFP.OR3 punctae were absent or strongly reduced in the presence of the RT inhibitors efavirenz (EFV) or azidothymidine (AZT).
source: eGFP.OR3 punctae were not detected when cells were treated with NNHIV ANCH lacking VSV-G and were absent or strongly reduced in the presence of the RT inhibitors efavirenz (EFV) or azidothymidine (AZT) (Figure 1f and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Experimental data showing dependence on reverse transcription.

claim: The onset of nuclear HIV-1 2-LTR detection using ddPCR coincided with the appearance of eGFP.OR3 punctae.
source: The onset of nuclear HIV-1 2-LTR detection using ddPCR coincided with the appearance of eGFP.OR3 punctae (Figure 1h).
evidence: Temporal correlation shown in Figure 1h.

claim: Formation of 2-LTR circles is dependent on nuclear NHEJ components and ligase IV.
source: Formation of both 2-LTR circles (dependent on nuclear NHEJ components and ligase IV [Li et al., 2001]) and eGFP.OR3 punctae requires viral cDNA to be synthesized and accessible to proteins not present in the subviral replication complex.
evidence: Citation to Li et al., 2001 supports this claim.

claim: A large proportion (~80%) of RT products detected by FISH was localized in the cytoplasm of infected cells.
source: A large proportion (~80%) of RT products detected by FISH was localized in the cytoplasm of infected cells, whereas no eGFP.OR3 punctae were observed in this compartment (Figure 2a; note that the harsh sample treatment required for FISH detection did not preserve eGFP.OR3 punctae, precluding analysis of both markers in the same specimen).
evidence: FISH quantification data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The number of nuclear FISH signals per cell (~14) was similar to the number of nuclear IN.SNAP signals (~12).
source: The number of nuclear FISH signals per cell (~14) (Figure 2a, right) was similar to the number of nuclear IN.SNAP signals (~12) (Figure 2b).
evidence: Quantification data from Figures 2a and 2b.

claim: Only ~4 nuclear eGFP.OR3 clusters were detected per cell.
source: In contrast, only ~4 nuclear eGFP.OR3 clusters were detected per cell (Figure 1f).
evidence: Quantification data from Figure 1f.

claim: The majority of late RT products – including all cytoplasmic products – were not associated with eGFP.OR3.
source: These results clearly showed that the majority of late RT products – including all cytoplasmic products – were not associated with eGFP.OR3.
evidence: Comparison of FISH signals, IN.SNAP signals, and eGFP.OR3 signals shows discrepancy.

claim: Co-localization with EdU was observed for 7% of IN-FP-positive structures in the cytoplasm.
source: Co-localization with EdU was observed for 7% of IN-FP-positive structures in the cytoplasm (95 % CI of mean: 4–9%) and for 36% of IN-FP-positive complexes in the nucleus (95 % CI of mean: 29–43%).
evidence: EdU incorporation experiment quantification.

claim: Co-localization with EdU was observed for 36% of IN-FP-positive complexes in the nucleus.
source: Co-localization with EdU was observed for 7% of IN-FP-positive structures in the cytoplasm (95 % CI of mean: 4–9%) and for 36% of IN-FP-positive complexes in the nucleus (95 % CI of mean: 29–43%).
evidence: EdU incorporation experiment quantification.

claim: 81% of nuclear eGFP.OR3 punctae were positive for EdU.
source: Importantly, 81% of nuclear eGFP.OR3 punctae were positive for EdU (95 % CI of mean: 70–93%; Figure 2d,e).
evidence: EdU incorporation experiment quantification shown in Figure 2e.

claim: The average EdU signal was lower on cytoplasmic than on nuclear HIV-1 complexes and was highest on eGFP.OR3 punctae.
source: The average EdU signal, as a correlate for reverse transcript length, was lower on cytoplasmic than on nuclear HIV-1 complexes and was highest on eGFP.OR3 punctae.
evidence: EdU signal intensity quantification shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The relative EdU signal was significantly reduced to 23% (p<0.0001) on cytoplasmic IN-FP-positive complexes compared to eGFP.OR3 punctae.
source: When setting the EdU signal for eGFP.OR3 punctae to 100%, the relative EdU signal was significantly reduced to 23% (p<0.0001) on cytoplasmic IN-FP-positive complexes and to 52% (p<0.0001) on nuclear IN-FP-positive complexes (Figure 2f).
evidence: Statistical analysis of EdU signal intensity data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The relative EdU signal was significantly reduced to 52% (p<0.0001) on nuclear IN-FP-positive complexes compared to eGFP.OR3 punctae.
source: When setting the EdU signal for eGFP.OR3 punctae to 100%, the relative EdU signal was significantly reduced to 23% (p<0.0001) on cytoplasmic IN-FP-positive complexes and to 52% (p<0.0001) on nuclear IN-FP-positive complexes (Figure 2f).
evidence: Statistical analysis of EdU signal intensity data shown in Figure 2f.

claim: Reverse transcription is completed inside the nucleus.
source: These observations support recent reports that reverse transcription is completed inside the nucleus (Burdick et al., 2020; Dharan et al., 2020; Francis et al., 2020; Selyutina et al., 2020) and indicate that the viral cDNA only becomes detectable to eGFP.OR3 when reverse transcription has been completed.
evidence: EdU data showing higher signal on nuclear complexes and citations to recent literature.

claim: The viral cDNA only becomes detectable to eGFP.OR3 when reverse transcription has been completed.
source: These observations support recent reports that reverse transcription is completed inside the nucleus (Burdick et al., 2020; Dharan et al., 2020; Francis et al., 2020; Selyutina et al., 2020) and indicate that the viral cDNA only becomes detectable to eGFP.OR3 when reverse transcription has been completed.
evidence: EdU signal is highest on eGFP.OR3 punctae, suggesting complete RT products.

claim: At 8 h p.i., 70 ± 11% of nuclear eGFP.OR3 punctae were also positive for IN.SNAP.
source: At 8 h p.i., 70 ± 11% of nuclear eGFP.OR3 punctae were also positive for IN.SNAP (Figure 3a–c).
evidence: Colocalization quantification data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: At 24 h p.i., only 14 ± 6% of nuclear eGFP.OR3 punctae were positive for IN.SNAP.
source: This co-localization was largely lost at 24 h p.i. with only 14 ± 6% of nuclear eGFP.OR3 punctae positive for IN.SNAP (Figure 3a–c).
evidence: Colocalization quantification data shown in Figure 3c.

claim: IN.SNAP punctae were often observed in close vicinity of eGFP.OR3 punctae at 24 h p.i.
source: Strikingly, IN.SNAP punctae were often observed in close vicinity of eGFP.OR3 punctae at this later time point (Figure 3a, right panel), suggesting that they may have separated from a common complex.
evidence: Microscopy images in Figure 3a showing spatial proximity.

claim: Live cell imaging showed gradual loss of the IN.SNAP signal correlating with increased eGFP.OR3 recruitment and eventual separation of eGFP.OR3 punctae and IN.SNAP containing complexes.
source: To directly address the possibility of separation of the proviral cDNA from IN.SNAP, we performed live cell imaging of infected cells. We observed gradual loss of the IN.SNAP signal correlating with increased eGFP.OR3 recruitment and eventual separation of eGFP.OR3 punctae and IN.SNAP containing complexes (Figure 3d,e, Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: Live cell imaging data shown in Figure 3d,e and video.

claim: Single diffraction limited IN.SNAP punctae may correspond to multiple cDNA containing subviral HIV-1 complexes.
source: Of note, we occasionally observed consecutive appearance of two individual eGFP.OR3 punctae and their subsequent separation from the same IN.SNAP complex (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—video 2), suggesting that single diffraction limited IN.SNAP punctae may correspond to multiple cDNA containing subviral HIV-1 complexes, indicating clustering of nuclear complexes as has been recently noted by others (Francis et al., 2020; Rensen et al., 2021).
evidence: Observation of two eGFP.OR3 punctae separating from one IN.SNAP complex.

claim: Methanol extraction following PFA fixation consistently yielded clear CA-specific signals co-localizing with most IN-FP-positive punctae inside the nucleus of TZM-bl cells.
source: While PFA fixation alone did not result in CA immunostaining of nuclear complexes (Figure 4a), methanol extraction (following PFA fixation) of parallel samples consistently yielded clear CA-specific signals co-localizing with most IN-FP-positive punctae inside the nucleus of TZM-bl cells (Figure 4b–c and Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data comparing PFA-only vs. PFA+methanol fixation shown in Figures 4a-c.

claim: IN-FP-positive punctae were strongly positive for the host protein CPSF6.
source: Furthermore, IN-FP-positive punctae were also strongly positive for the host protein cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor 6 (CPSF6) that binds specifically to the hexameric CA lattice (Bhattacharya et al., 2014; Price et al., 2014; Figure 4d) and is involved in nuclear import (Bejarano et al., 2019; Burdick et al., 2020; Chin et al., 2015), trafficking to nuclear speckles (Francis et al., 2020; Rensen et al., 2021) and integration-site targeting (Achuthan et al., 2018; Francis et al., 2020; Sowd et al., 2016).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4d and citations to literature on CPSF6 function.

claim: CPSF6 binds specifically to the hexameric CA lattice.
source: Furthermore, IN-FP-positive punctae were also strongly positive for the host protein cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor 6 (CPSF6) that binds specifically to the hexameric CA lattice (Bhattacharya et al., 2014; Price et al., 2014; Figure 4d) and is involved in nuclear import (Bejarano et al., 2019; Burdick et al., 2020; Chin et al., 2015), trafficking to nuclear speckles (Francis et al., 2020; Rensen et al., 2021) and integration-site targeting (Achuthan et al., 2018; Francis et al., 2020; Sowd et al., 2016).
evidence: Citations to Bhattacharya et al., 2014 and Price et al., 2014.

claim: CPSF6 is involved in nuclear import of HIV-1 complexes.
source: Furthermore, IN-FP-positive punctae were also strongly positive for the host protein cleavage and polyadenylation specificity factor 6 (CPSF6) that binds specifically to the hexameric CA lattice (Bhattacharya et al., 2014; Price et al., 2014; Figure 4d) and is involved in nuclear import (Bejarano et al., 2019; Burdick et al., 2020; Chin et al., 2015), trafficking to nuclear speckles (Francis et al., 2020; Rensen et al., 2021) and integration-site targeting (Achuthan et al., 2018; Francis et al., 2020; Sowd et al., 2016).
evidence: Citations to Bejarano et al., 2019; Burdick et al., 2020; Chin et al., 2015.

claim: PF74 acts as a competitive inhibitor of CA-CPSF6 interaction.
source: This hypothesis was tested by treating infected cells - after the subviral complexes had entered the nucleus – with the small molecule PF74, which acts as a competitive inhibitor of CA-CPSF6 interaction (Price et al., 2014) and may thus displace CPSF6 from the subviral complex.
evidence: Citation to Price et al., 2014.

claim: PF74 treatment resulted in a dose-dependent loss of CPSF6 signal from nuclear HIV-1 subviral complexes.
source: We observed a dose-dependent loss of CPSF6 signal from nuclear HIV-1 subviral complexes upon PF74 treatment, while IN-FP punctae stayed intact (Figure 4e and g, left panel).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: PF74-mediated removal of CPSF6 from the nuclear subviral complexes revealed a strong CA IF signal.
source: PF74-mediated removal of CPSF6 from the nuclear subviral complexes revealed a strong CA IF signal (Figure 4f), with inverse correlation of CPSF6 and CA signal intensities (Figure 4g, right panel).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 4f and 4g.

claim: CPSF6 displacement occurred rapidly, within 30 min of PF74 treatment.
source: CPSF6 displacement occurred rapidly, within 30 min of PF74 treatment (Figure 4h).
evidence: Time course data shown in Figure 4h.

claim: CA immunostaining intensities of particles outside of the nucleus were not affected by PF74 treatment.
source: CA immunostaining intensities of particles outside of the nucleus were not affected by PF74 treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b), suggesting that the enhanced CA signal on nuclear complexes was not due to structural changes in the capsid lattice induced by the drug.
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b.

claim: CPSF6 shields CA from antibody detection inside the nucleus.
source: We conclude that CPSF6 shields CA from antibody detection inside the nucleus and CA signal intensity on nuclear complexes is comparable to that on cytoplasmic complexes in HeLa-derived cells.
evidence: PF74 displacement of CPSF6 reveals CA signal, suggesting CPSF6 was masking epitopes.

claim: CA signal intensity on nuclear complexes is comparable to that on cytoplasmic complexes in HeLa-derived cells.
source: We conclude that CPSF6 shields CA from antibody detection inside the nucleus and CA signal intensity on nuclear complexes is comparable to that on cytoplasmic complexes in HeLa-derived cells.
evidence: Quantification data comparing CA intensities at different cellular locations.

claim: Nuclear HIV-1 complexes displayed similar CA intensities compared to extranuclear particles in cells that had not undergone division.
source: We clearly detected HIV-1 complexes in the nuclei of cells that had not undergone division during the observation period. These nuclear complexes displayed similar CA intensities compared to extranuclear particles (Figure 4n and o), supporting the conclusion that subviral complexes comprising most or all of the CA complement of the viral capsid can pass through intact nuclear pores in HeLa-derived cells.
evidence: Live imaging followed by IF staining and quantification shown in Figures 4n and 4o.

claim: Subviral complexes comprising most or all of the CA complement of the viral capsid can pass through intact nuclear pores in HeLa-derived cells.
source: We clearly detected HIV-1 complexes in the nuclei of cells that had not undergone division during the observation period. These nuclear complexes displayed similar CA intensities compared to extranuclear particles (Figure 4n and o), supporting the conclusion that subviral complexes comprising most or all of the CA complement of the viral capsid can pass through intact nuclear pores in HeLa-derived cells.
evidence: CA intensity data from non-dividing cells supports this conclusion.

claim: The mature HIV-1 capsid contains ca. 50% of the total CA content of the intact virion.
source: The mature HIV-1 capsid contains ca. 50% of the total CA content of the intact virion and post-fusion cytoplasmic capsids therefore exhibit a weaker CA signal than complete virions (Briggs et al., 2004; Zila et al., 2019).
evidence: Citations to Briggs et al., 2004 and Zila et al., 2019.

claim: Post-fusion cytoplasmic capsids exhibit a weaker CA signal than complete virions.
source: The mature HIV-1 capsid contains ca. 50% of the total CA content of the intact virion and post-fusion cytoplasmic capsids therefore exhibit a weaker CA signal than complete virions (Briggs et al., 2004; Zila et al., 2019).
evidence: Citations to Briggs et al., 2004 and Zila et al., 2019.

claim: The observed intensity of the CA signal on nuclear HIV-1 complexes was equal to the intensities observed for cell-associated particles.
source: However, the observed intensity of the CA signal on nuclear HIV-1 complexes was equal to the intensities observed for cell-associated particles (Figure 4b).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Multiple individual CA signals in close vicinity to each other could be resolved within the area of a single focus detected in confocal mode using STED nanoscopy.
source: In order to investigate this possibility, we used STED nanoscopy to resolve individual subviral structures with a resolution of <50 nm. Multiple individual CA signals in close vicinity to each other could be resolved within the area of a single focus detected in confocal mode (Figure 5a and b).
evidence: STED microscopy data shown in Figures 5a and 5b.

claim: IN.SNAP-positive and eGFP.OR3-negative nuclear punctae detected by fluorescence microscopy could be correlated with single or multiple electron-dense cone-shaped structures, whose shapes and dimensions closely resembled mature HIV-1 capsids.
source: IN.SNAP-positive and eGFP.OR3-negative nuclear punctae detected by fluorescence microscopy could be correlated with single or multiple electron-dense cone-shaped structures, whose shapes and dimensions closely resembled mature HIV-1 capsids (Figure 5c, Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: CLEM-ET data shown in Figure 5c.

claim: STED nanoscopy of nuclear SNAP.OR3-positive punctae corresponding to viral cDNA identified elongated structures.
source: STED nanoscopy of nuclear SNAP.OR3-positive punctae corresponding to viral cDNA identified elongated structures (Figure 5d); in this case, only a single object was resolved by STED nanoscopy at each diffraction-limited position.
evidence: STED microscopy data shown in Figure 5d.

claim: A total of 21 individual structures were identified and visualized by CLEM-ET covering the volume of six individual nuclei.
source: A total of 21 individual structures were identified and visualized by CLEM-ET covering the volume of six individual nuclei (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: CLEM-ET data summarized in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: The majority of structures (20/21; 95%) was found in clusters of two or more structures.
source: The majority of structures (20/21; 95%) was found in clusters of two or more structures.
evidence: CLEM-ET data analysis.

claim: At positions correlating to IN-positive punctae lacking mScarlet.OR3 (18/21; 86%), we detected 10 cone-shaped structures resembling intact HIV-1 capsids.
source: At positions correlating to IN-positive punctae lacking mScarlet.OR3 (18/21; 86%), we detected 10 cone-shaped structures resembling intact HIV-1 capsids (Figures 5c and 6g ii. and 6i.) and eight structures with less defined morphology consistent with deformed tubular structures or remnants of capsids (Figure 6g ii and 6h ii; Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: CLEM-ET data shown in Figures 5c, 6g, 6h, 6i.

claim: At positions correlating to IN-positive punctae lacking mScarlet.OR3, we detected eight structures with less defined morphology consistent with deformed tubular structures or remnants of capsids.
source: At positions correlating to IN-positive punctae lacking mScarlet.OR3 (18/21; 86%), we detected 10 cone-shaped structures resembling intact HIV-1 capsids (Figures 5c and 6g ii. and 6i.) and eight structures with less defined morphology consistent with deformed tubular structures or remnants of capsids (Figure 6g ii and 6h ii; Figure 6—video 1).
evidence: CLEM-ET data shown in Figures 6g and 6h.

claim: Dense material most likely corresponding to the viral nucleoprotein complex was visible inside of most conical structures.
source: Dense material most likely corresponding to the viral nucleoprotein complex was visible inside of most conical structures (Figures 5c and 6g ii. and 6i top left panel, black arrowheads), whereas tubular and capsid remnant-like structures mostly lacked interior densities (Figure 6g ii., 6h ii. and 6i bottom left panel, open white arrowheads).
evidence: Electron tomography observations shown in Figures 5c, 6g, 6i.

claim: Tubular and capsid remnant-like structures mostly lacked interior densities.
source: Dense material most likely corresponding to the viral nucleoprotein complex was visible inside of most conical structures (Figures 5c and 6g ii. and 6i top left panel, black arrowheads), whereas tubular and capsid remnant-like structures mostly lacked interior densities (Figure 6g ii., 6h ii. and 6i bottom left panel, open white arrowheads).
evidence: Electron tomography observations shown in Figures 6g, 6h, 6i.

claim: Electron tomograms that correlated to positions of mScarlet.OR3 signals (lacking IN.SNAP.SiR signal; n = 7) showed no defined conical or capsid remnant-like structures.
source: In contrast, electron tomograms that correlated to positions of mScarlet.OR3 signals (lacking IN.SNAP.SiR signal; n = 7) showed no defined conical or capsid remnant-like structures.
evidence: CLEM-ET data analysis.

claim: Elongated dense objects of ~100–300 nm in length were observed at positions of mScarlet.OR3 signals lacking IN.SNAP.SiR signal.
source: Instead, elongated dense objects of ~100–300 nm in length were observed (Figure 6g i. and 6h i.), in line with the findings from STED nanoscopy (compare Figure 5d).
evidence: Electron tomography data shown in Figures 6g and 6h.

claim: Elongated structures at OR3-positive positions consisted of linked globular densities with a diameter of ~30 nm resembling the appearance of chromatin.
source: These structures consisted of linked globular densities with a diameter of ~30 nm resembling the appearance of chromatin (Figure 6h i.).
evidence: Electron tomography data shown in Figure 6h.

claim: Infection of an eGFP.OR3 expressing SupT1 cell line with NNHIV ANCH showed nuclear OR3 punctae and separation of IN-FP and OR3 punctae as observed for TZM-bl cells.
source: Infection of an eGFP.OR3 expressing SupT1 cell line (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) or of primary activated CD4+ T cells transduced to express eGFP.OR3 (Figure 7a) with NNHIV ANCH showed nuclear OR3 punctae and separation of IN-FP and OR3 punctae as observed for TZM-bl cells.
evidence: Microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7a.

claim: Infection of primary activated CD4+ T cells transduced to express eGFP.OR3 with NNHIV ANCH showed nuclear OR3 punctae and separation of IN-FP and OR3 punctae as observed for TZM-bl cells.
source: Infection of an eGFP.OR3 expressing SupT1 cell line (Figure 7—figure supplement 1) or of primary activated CD4+ T cells transduced to express eGFP.OR3 (Figure 7a) with NNHIV ANCH showed nuclear OR3 punctae and separation of IN-FP and OR3 punctae as observed for TZM-bl cells.
evidence: Microscopy data shown in Figure 7a.

claim: No or weak CA signals were detected co-localizing with IN.SNAP punctae in T cells, even upon methanol extraction.
source: In accordance with previous observations (Zila et al., 2019), no or weak CA signals were detected co-localizing with IN.SNAP punctae in T cells (Figure 7a), even upon methanol extraction.
evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7a and citation to Zila et al., 2019.

claim: Strong signals for CPSF6 were detected at positions of IN-FP in T cells.
source: However, similarly to observations in HeLa-based cells (Figure 4d), strong signals for CPSF6 were detected at positions of IN-FP (Figure 7b top panel).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: Displacing CPSF6 from nuclear subviral particles using PF74 revealed a strong CA IF signal in T cells.
source: Displacing this CPSF6 coat from the nuclear subviral particles using PF74 (Figure 7b–c) as described above, strikingly revealed a strong CA IF signal (Figure 7d–f).
evidence: Immunofluorescence data shown in Figures 7b-f.

claim: Detection of nuclear CA in T cells depended on a combination of PF74 treatment and methanol extraction of specimens.
source: Of note, detection of nuclear CA in T cells depended on a combination of PF74 treatment and methanol extraction of specimens (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), while either treatment alone was sufficient to expose CA in HeLa-derived cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a–b).
evidence: Comparison of treatment conditions shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: No difference was observed for CA IF signals on extracellular particles and on cytoplasmic or nuclear envelope-associated subviral complexes upon PF74 treatment in T cells.
source: In agreement with results from HeLa-based cells, no difference was observed for CA IF signals on extracellular particles and on cytoplasmic or nuclear envelope-associated subviral complexes upon PF74 treatment, while the nuclear CA signal became strongly enhanced (Figure 7e–f).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figures 7e-f.

claim: The failure to detect nuclear CA by IF in CD4+ T cells is due to shielding of epitopes by the accumulation of CPSF6 rather than to CA being lost upon nuclear entry in these cells.
source: Thus, the failure to detect nuclear CA by IF in CD4+ T cells is due to shielding of epitopes by the accumulation of CPSF6 rather than to CA being lost upon nuclear entry in these cells, in accordance with our recent cryo-ET analyses in SupT1 cells (Zila et al., 2021).
evidence: PF74 displacement of CPSF6 reveals CA signal, and citation to Zila et al., 2021.

claim: Nuclear subviral complexes showed a higher mean CA signal compared to complete virions in T cells.
source: Of note, nuclear subviral complexes showed a higher mean CA signal compared to complete virions, consistent with nuclear clustering of CA containing complexes (Francis et al., 2020; Rensen et al., 2021) also in this cell type; this was most evident at earlier time points (Figure 7e–f).
evidence: Quantification data shown in Figures 7e-f and citations to Francis et al., 2020 and Rensen et al., 2021.

claim: After PF74 treatment, some nuclear eGFP.OR3 punctae representing HIV-1 cDNA were associated with IN-FP and strongly CA positive in primary CD4+ T cells.
source: After PF74 treatment we could also observe some nuclear eGFP.OR3 punctae representing HIV-1 cDNA that were associated with IN-FP and strongly CA positive (Figure 7g).
evidence: Microscopy data shown in Figure 7g.

claim: Upon separation from eGFP.OR3 punctae, CPSF6 clusters remained associated with the IN-FP in primary CD4+ T cells.
source: Upon separation from eGFP.OR3 punctae, CPSF6 clusters remained associated with the IN-FP, confirming that the viral cDNA separates from an IN-FP/CA/CPSF6-positive nuclear structure in the nucleus of infected primary CD4+ T cells as well (Figure 7h).
evidence: Microscopy data shown in Figure 7h.

claim: A similar phenotype as shown for TZM-bl cells and primary CD4+ T cells was observed in MDM: the majority of eGFP.O3 punctae was detected separated from, but often in close vicinity of IN.mScarlet punctae.
source: A similar phenotype as shown above for TZM-bl cells and primary CD4+ T cells was observed in MDM: the majority of eGFP.O3 punctae was detected separated from, but often in close vicinity of IN.mScarlet punctae (Figure 7i).
evidence: Microscopy data shown in Figure 7i.

claim: Both integrated and unintegrated HIV-1 cDNA were detected by OR3 in the nucleus.
source: Both, integrated and unintegrated HIV-1 cDNA were detected by OR3 in the nucleus.
evidence: Experiments with integration-competent and integration-deficient viruses both showed nuclear OR3 punctae.

claim: Nuclear eGFP.OR3 punctae contained significantly higher DNA amounts compared to cytoplasmic or nuclear subviral complexes lacking the eGFP.OR3 signal.
source: Metabolic labeling of nascent DNA revealed that nuclear eGFP.OR3 punctae contained significantly higher DNA amounts compared to cytoplasmic or nuclear subviral complexes lacking the eGFP.OR3 signal.
evidence: EdU incorporation data showing higher signal on eGFP.OR3 punctae.

claim: HIV-1 cDNA separated from an IN fusion protein (IN-FP) inside the nucleus.
source: Furthermore, HIV-1 cDNA separated from an IN fusion protein (IN-FP), often used as a marker for the HIV-1 replication complex, inside the nucleus; IN fusions are thus not suitable for tracking HIV-1 cDNA in the nucleus.
evidence: Live cell imaging and fixed cell data showing separation of IN-FP and eGFP.OR3 signals.

claim: IN fusions are not suitable for tracking HIV-1 cDNA in the nucleus.
source: Furthermore, HIV-1 cDNA separated from an IN fusion protein (IN-FP), often used as a marker for the HIV-1 replication complex, inside the nucleus; IN fusions are thus not suitable for tracking HIV-1 cDNA in the nucleus.
evidence: Separation of IN-FP from cDNA marker indicates IN-FP does not track with cDNA.

claim: Nuclear IN-FP punctae were strongly positive for the viral CA protein.
source: Nuclear IN-FP punctae were strongly positive for the viral CA protein and CA, CPSF6 and IN-FP signals stayed together after separation from the viral cDNA.
evidence: Immunofluorescence data showing colocalization of IN-FP, CA, and CPSF6.

claim: CA, CPSF6 and IN-FP signals stayed together after separation from the viral cDNA.
source: Nuclear IN-FP punctae were strongly positive for the viral CA protein and CA, CPSF6 and IN-FP signals stayed together after separation from the viral cDNA.
evidence: Microscopy data showing these markers remain colocalized after cDNA separation.

claim: OR3 recruitment to the HIV-1 cDNA requires the dsDNA to be accessible to the 66 kDa eGFP.OR3 fusion protein, which depends on loss of integrity of the capsid shell.
source: OR3 recruitment to the HIV-1 cDNA requires the dsDNA to be accessible to the 66 kDa eGFP.OR3 fusion protein, which depends on loss of integrity of the capsid shell.
evidence: The size of the fusion protein and requirement for DNA accessibility implies capsid opening is necessary.

claim: CA signal intensity on nuclear IN-FP-positive and eGFP.OR3-negative structures was equal to or higher than observed for cytoplasmic complexes.
source: CA signal intensity on nuclear IN-FP-positive and eGFP.OR3-negative structures was equal to or higher than observed for cytoplasmic complexes, suggesting that the bulk of CA stays associated with the viral replication complex and the viral DNA remains encased inside a closed capsid or capsid-like structure until after nuclear entry.
evidence: Quantification of CA signal intensities at different cellular locations.

claim: The bulk of CA stays associated with the viral replication complex and the viral DNA remains encased inside a closed capsid or capsid-like structure until after nuclear entry.
source: CA signal intensity on nuclear IN-FP-positive and eGFP.OR3-negative structures was equal to or higher than observed for cytoplasmic complexes, suggesting that the bulk of CA stays associated with the viral replication complex and the viral DNA remains encased inside a closed capsid or capsid-like structure until after nuclear entry.
evidence: High CA signal on nuclear complexes suggests intact or largely intact capsid.

claim: Apparently intact cone-shaped HIV-1 capsids can enter the nucleus through intact nuclear pores.
source: This finding is consistent with our recent study showing that the nuclear pore channel is sufficiently large to accommodate the HIV-1 core and apparently intact cone-shaped HIV-1 capsids can enter the nucleus through intact nuclear pores (Zila et al., 2021).
evidence: Citation to Zila et al., 2021 and CLEM-ET data showing intact capsids in nucleus.

claim: Reverse transcription initiates in the cytoplasm inside a complete or largely complete capsid.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that reverse transcription initiates in the cytoplasm inside a complete or largely complete capsid, and this capsid-encased complex traffics into the nucleus, where reverse transcription is completed; subsequently, it must be uncoated for integration to occur.
evidence: Integration of multiple observations about RT timing, nuclear entry, and capsid integrity.

claim: The capsid-encased complex traffics into the nucleus, where reverse transcription is completed.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that reverse transcription initiates in the cytoplasm inside a complete or largely complete capsid, and this capsid-encased complex traffics into the nucleus, where reverse transcription is completed; subsequently, it must be uncoated for integration to occur.
evidence: EdU data and timing of OR3 recruitment support nuclear completion of RT.

claim: Formation of eGFP.OR3 punctae requires both completion of reverse transcription and at least partial uncoating.
source: Formation of eGFP.OR3 punctae requires both, completion of reverse transcription and – at least partial – uncoating, and these two events may conceivably occur in a coordinated manner.
evidence: OR3 requires accessible dsDNA, which requires both complete RT and capsid opening.

claim: Viral cDNA associated with some replication proteins emanates from the broken capsid, which retains the bulk of CA and capsid-associated proteins.
source: These results indicate that viral cDNA associated with some replication proteins emanates from the broken capsid, which retains the bulk of CA and capsid-associated proteins.
evidence: CLEM-ET showing broken capsids near cDNA and CA remaining with IN-FP complexes.

claim: Uncoating does not appear to occur by cooperative disassembly of the CA lattice, but by physically breaking the capsid shell and loss of irregular capsid segments.
source: Uncoating therefore does not appear to occur by cooperative disassembly of the CA lattice, but by physically breaking the capsid shell and loss of irregular capsid segments.
evidence: CLEM-ET showing broken capsid structures rather than gradual disassembly.

claim: Clustering of capsids or capsid-remnants inside the nucleus indicates preferred trafficking routes of subviral complexes.
source: We often observed clustering of capsids or capsid-remnants inside the nucleus indicating preferred trafficking routes of subviral complexes, as described by others (Francis et al., 2020; Rensen et al., 2021).
evidence: CLEM-ET data showing multiple structures in close proximity and citations to Francis et al., 2020 and Rensen et al., 2021.

claim: The broken capsid-remnant structures inside the nucleus of infected cells closely resembled ruptured HIV-1 cores observed in an in vitro system analyzing HIV-1 cDNA formation and integration.
source: The broken capsid-remnant structures inside the nucleus of infected cells closely resembled ruptured HIV-1 cores observed in a recent study analyzing HIV-1 cDNA formation and integration in an in vitro system using purified virions (Christensen et al., 2020).
evidence: Citation to Christensen et al., 2020 and comparison of morphologies.

claim: The growing dsDNA inside the viral capsid in the nucleus may eventually lead to local rupture of the capsid lattice, concomitantly allowing completion of reverse transcription and triggering uncoating of the proviral DNA.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the growing dsDNA inside the viral capsid in the nucleus may eventually lead to local rupture of the capsid lattice, concomitantly allowing completion of reverse transcription and triggering uncoating of the proviral DNA.
evidence: Integration of observations about broken capsids, dsDNA volume constraints, and theoretical models.

claim: The described pathway of nuclear uncoating appears to be conserved in HeLa reporter cells and primary HIV-1-sensitive CD4+ T-cells and MDM.
source: The described pathway appears to be conserved in HeLa reporter cells and primary HIV-1-sensitive CD4+ T-cells and MDM: separation of IN/CA complexes from the OR3-positive cDNA inside the nucleus of infected cells was observed in all cell types, and the IN-positive subviral complexes exhibited a strong CA signal in all cases.
evidence: Data from multiple cell types showing similar phenotypes.

claim: Previous failure to detect CA on nuclear complexes in T cells has been due to epitope masking by the cellular CPSF6 protein.
source: Previous failure to detect CA on nuclear complexes in T cells has been due to epitope masking by the cellular CPSF6 protein and the current results thus indicate a common pathway for early HIV-1 replication in different cell types including primary target cells of HIV-1 infection.
evidence: PF74 displacement of CPSF6 reveals CA signal in T cells.

claim: Complete or largely complete HIV-1 capsids enter the nucleus of infected cells, where reverse transcription is completed and the viral cDNA genome is released by physical disruption rather than by cooperative disassembly of the capsid lattice.
source: In conclusion, our results indicate that complete or largely complete HIV-1 capsids enter the nucleus of infected cells, where reverse transcription is completed and the viral cDNA genome is released by physical disruption rather than by cooperative disassembly of the capsid lattice (Figure 8).
evidence: Summary of multiple lines of evidence from the study.

claim: The viral capsid plays an active role in the entire early phase of HIV-1 replication up to chromosomal integration.
source: The viral capsid thus plays an active role in the entire early phase of HIV-1 replication up to chromosomal integration and appears to be important for cytoplasmic trafficking, reverse transcription, shielding of viral nucleic acid from the innate immune system, nuclear entry, and intranuclear trafficking.
evidence: Integration of findings showing capsid presence throughout early replication and citations to literature on capsid functions.

claim: The cone-shaped HIV-1 capsid with its fullerene geometry is the key orchestrator of early HIV-1 replication.
source: The cone-shaped HIV-1 capsid with its fullerene geometry thus is the key orchestrator of early HIV-1 replication.
evidence: Summary statement based on the role of capsid throughout early replication.

claim: The HIV-1 capsid, with a length of ~120 nm and a width of ~60 nm at its wide end, is presumed to exceed the dimensions of the NPC channel with a reported maximal diameter of ~40 nm.
source: However, the HIV-1 capsid, with a length of ~120 nm and a width of ~60 nm at its wide end (Mattei et al., 2016), is presumed to exceed the dimensions of the NPC channel with a reported maximal diameter of ~40 nm (von Appen et al., 2015).
evidence: Citations to Mattei et al., 2016 and von Appen et al., 2015 for capsid and NPC dimensions.

claim: Various publications reported uncoating either in the cytoplasm or at the nuclear pore, with some evidence for cell-type-dependent differences.
source: This implies that capsid uncoating should occur – at least partially – prior to nuclear entry, and various publications reported uncoating either in the cytoplasm (Cosnefroy et al., 2016; Hulme et al., 2011; Mamede et al., 2017; Xu et al., 2013) or at the nuclear pore (Arhel et al., 2007; Burdick et al., 2017; Francis and Melikyan, 2018), with some evidence for cell-type-dependent differences.
evidence: Citations to multiple studies reporting different uncoating locations.

claim: Nuclear HIV-1 pre-integration complexes (PIC) were found to retain varying amounts of CA molecules.
source: On the other hand, nuclear HIV-1 pre-integration complexes (PIC) were found to retain varying amounts of CA molecules (Bejarano et al., 2019; Burdick et al., 2020; Chin et al., 2015; Hulme et al., 2015; Stultz et al., 2017; Zila et al., 2019), at least in certain cell types (Zila et al., 2019), and recent reports indicating the presence of intact capsid lattice (Dharan et al., 2020; Selyutina et al., 2020) and capsid-like structures (Zila et al., 2021) inside the nucleus challenged the current models of early HIV-1 replication.
evidence: Citations to multiple studies detecting CA in nuclear complexes.

claim: Recent reports indicate the presence of intact capsid lattice inside the nucleus.
source: On the other hand, nuclear HIV-1 pre-integration complexes (PIC) were found to retain varying amounts of CA molecules (Bejarano et al., 2019; Burdick et al., 2020; Chin et al., 2015; Hulme et al., 2015; Stultz et al., 2017; Zila et al., 2019), at least in certain cell types (Zila et al., 2019), and recent reports indicating the presence of intact capsid lattice (Dharan et al., 2020; Selyutina et al., 2020) and capsid-like structures (Zila et al., 2021) inside the nucleus challenged the current models of early HIV-1 replication.
evidence: Citations to Dharan et al., 2020 and Selyutina et al., 2020.

claim: Recent reports indicate the presence of capsid-like structures inside the nucleus.
source: On the other hand, nuclear HIV-1 pre-integration complexes (PIC) were found to retain varying amounts of CA molecules (Bejarano et al., 2019; Burdick et al., 2020; Chin et al., 2015; Hulme et al., 2015; Stultz et al., 2017; Zila et al., 2019), at least in certain cell types (Zila et al., 2019), and recent reports indicating the presence of intact capsid lattice (Dharan et al., 2020; Selyutina et al., 2020) and capsid-like structures (Zila et al., 2021) inside the nucleus challenged the current models of early HIV-1 replication.
evidence: Citation to Zila et al., 2021.

claim: The timing, subcellular localization, trigger and mechanism of HIV-1 capsid uncoating are still under debate.
source: Accordingly, the timing, subcellular localization, trigger and mechanism of HIV-1 capsid uncoating are still under debate.
evidence: Summary of conflicting reports in the literature.

claim: Most cytoplasmic entry events appear to be non-productive in tissue culture.
source: Studying early HIV-1 replication is hampered by the fact that most cytoplasmic entry events appear to be non-productive in tissue culture (Klasse, 2015; Sanjuán, 2018).
evidence: Citations to Klasse, 2015 and Sanjuán, 2018.

claim: The ANCHOR system is based on the prokaryotic chromosomal partitioning system ParB-parS, where ParB (designated OR) specifically binds the parS seed sequence (designated ANCH).
source: This system is based on the prokaryotic chromosomal partitioning system ParB-parS, where ParB (designated OR) specifically binds the parS seed sequence (designated ANCH).
evidence: Description of the ANCHOR system mechanism.

claim: Multiple copies of parS introduced into the HIV-1 genome act as nucleation sites to oligomerize the fluorescently labeled OR protein when the reverse transcribed ANCH cDNA sequence becomes accessible to the fusion protein.
source: Multiple copies of parS introduced into the HIV-1 genome act as nucleation sites to oligomerize the fluorescently labeled OR protein when the reverse transcribed ANCH cDNA sequence becomes accessible to the fusion protein.
evidence: Description of how the ANCHOR system works for HIV-1 cDNA detection.

claim: The ANCHOR system has been applied for visualization of DNA from Adenovirus, Cytomegalovirus, and HIV-1.
source: To overcome these limitations, we adapted a live cell compatible genetically encoded system (ANCHOR) that allows single-molecule gene labeling (Germier et al., 2017; Saad et al., 2014), and has been applied for visualization of DNA from Adenovirus (Komatsu et al., 2018), Cytomegalovirus (Mariamé et al., 2018), and HIV-1 (Blanco-Rodriguez et al., 2020).
evidence: Citations to studies using ANCHOR for different viruses.

claim: The onset of nuclear HIV-1 2-LTR detection using ddPCR coincided with the appearance of eGFP.OR3 punctae, with half-maximal signal reached between 13 and 15 h p.i.
source: The onset of nuclear HIV-1 2-LTR detection using ddPCR coincided with the appearance of eGFP.OR3 punctae (Figure 1h).
evidence: Temporal correlation data shown in Figure 1h.

claim: The lack of cytoplasmic eGFP.OR3 punctae may be due to incomplete cDNA synthesis in the cytoplasm and/or to shielding of the cDNA from the fusion protein until full capsid uncoating in the nucleus.
source: Accordingly, the lack of cytoplasmic eGFP.OR3 punctae may be due to incomplete cDNA synthesis in the cytoplasm and/or to shielding of the cDNA from the fusion protein until full capsid uncoating in the nucleus.
evidence: Inference from the observation that OR3 punctae only appear in nucleus despite cytoplasmic RT products.

claim: The efficiency of CA immunostaining in the nucleus appears to be partially dependent on the cell type.
source: The efficiency of CA immunostaining in the nucleus appears to be partially dependent on the cell type.
evidence: Comparison of staining requirements across different cell types.

claim: In MDMs and THP-1 cells, nuclear CA signals were detected by immunofluorescence upon copper-click-mediated cellular extraction without CPSF6-removal.
source: In MDMs (Bejarano et al., 2018; Stultz et al., 2017; Zila et al., 2019) and THP-1 cells (Rensen et al., 2021), nuclear CA signals were detected by immunofluorescence upon copper-click-mediated cellular extraction without CPSF6-removal.
evidence: Citations to studies detecting nuclear CA in these cell types.

claim: In HeLa-derived cells, immunostaining of nuclear CA could be recovered by either methanol extraction or PF74-mediated CPSF6 displacement.
source: In HeLa-derived cells, immunostaining of nuclear CA could be recovered by either methanol extraction or PF74-mediated CPSF6 displacement, whereas a combination of methanol extraction and PF74 treatment was necessary in T-cells.
evidence: Experimental data comparing treatment requirements across cell types.

claim: A combination of methanol extraction and PF74 treatment was necessary to detect nuclear CA in T-cells.
source: In HeLa-derived cells, immunostaining of nuclear CA could be recovered by either methanol extraction or PF74-mediated CPSF6 displacement, whereas a combination of methanol extraction and PF74 treatment was necessary in T-cells.
evidence: Experimental data from T cell experiments.

claim: Strong CA signals resembling the intensity on cytoplasmic subviral HIV-1 complexes were detected in all cell types.
source: Nevertheless, strong CA signals resembling the intensity on cytoplasmic subviral HIV-1 complexes were detected in all cell types indicating a common pathway for nuclear entry of capsid-containing HIV-1 replication structures.
evidence: Quantification data from multiple cell types.

claim: Chromatinization of HIV-1 cDNA emerging from the broken capsid may facilitate complete uncoating of the genome.
source: We suggest that chromatinization of HIV-1 cDNA emerging from the broken capsid may facilitate complete uncoating of the genome, which could explain why viral cDNA remained largely associated with the capsid structure in the in vitro system.
evidence: Speculation based on chromatin-like structures observed at OR3-positive positions and comparison to in vitro data.

claim: HIV-1 cDNA is rapidly chromatinized when it becomes accessible to the nucleoplasm.
source: These structures resembled chromatinized DNA (Miron et al., 2020), in line with biochemical evidence that HIV-1 cDNA is rapidly chromatinized when it becomes accessible to the nucleoplasm (Geis and Goff, 2019).
evidence: Citation to Geis and Goff, 2019 and comparison to chromatin morphology.
